compound_name: Tetrachloridodioxidouranate(VI) ion, [UO2Cl4]2-, the complex anion of cesium uranyl chloride
ligand_set: two axial oxido ligands forming the linear uranyl unit and four equatorial chlorides
geometry_source: Geometries imposed by hand rather than optimized - the U-O distance is scanned sequentially over 1.75-1.80 angstrom and the U-Cl distance over 2.40-2.68 angstrom, the ranges expected under the applied pressures; the experimental crystal structure is used for the one validation point against measured charge density
method: CASSCF wave functions used to generate electron densities for a quantum-theory-of-atoms-in-molecules topological analysis, and to produce molecular orbital plots for comparison against density functional ones; scalar-relativistic PBE0 supplies the starting orbitals
software: ORCA 4.0 for the electronic-structure calculations; AIMAll for the topological analysis
basis_set: SARC-TZVP on uranium and def2-TZVP on all other atoms, as stated for the density functional step that supplies the starting orbitals; the text does not separately state the basis for the correlated step
relativistic_treatment: second-order all-electron Douglas-Kroll-Hess Hamiltonian
active_space_protocol: The space is defined by a criterion rather than a count: the f and d orbitals of uranium 'that had significant bonding with the O atoms'. No number of electrons or orbitals is given anywhere in the body text, nor which specific f and d orbitals qualified. Orbitals from a preceding scalar-relativistic hybrid density functional calculation are used as the starting wave function. Note that the selection criterion references the U-O bond while the conclusion concerns U-Cl covalency, so the space is aligned with one side of the comparison. No perturbative correction, no root count, no multiplicities, no state averaging, no IPEA or level shift is reported. The resulting wave functions are used solely to generate densities for a topological atoms-in-molecules analysis and to produce orbital plots.
electronic_structure_description: The uranyl(VI) ion with four equatorial chlorides, formally 5f0 and closed shell, whose short strongly covalent axial U-O bonds dominate its chemistry. The question addressed is how those axial bonds respond to compression of the equatorial U-Cl bonds. Covalency is quantified by the covalency degree, the total energy density per electron at the bond critical point. Validating against experiment at the crystal geometry gives -0.92 hartree/angstrom for the calculated U-O covalency degree against -0.93 from the measured charge density. Across the scans, shortening U-O makes the U-O covalency degree linearly more negative, while shortening U-Cl changes the U-O covalency degree only very slightly - the basis for the claim that the uranyl bond is almost unaffected by the equatorial bond and that earlier density functional work overestimated the coupling. The orbital comparison behind that claim is qualitative: density functional orbitals show significantly more chloride involvement than the CASSCF ones, attributed to the known tendency of density functional methods to overdelocalize.
Other: What the multireference calculation actually produced is far less than the abstract implies. The abstract credits 'ab initio wave function methods (CASSCF)' with supporting the claim that the uranyl bond is sensitive to its own length but negligibly affected by the U-Cl length. In fact the CASSCF supplies no energies, no excited states and no spectroscopy. Its entire output is a set of wave functions handed to a topological electron-density analysis, plus orbital pictures compared side by side against density functional ones. Every quantitative result in the paper - the Raman shift with pressure, the linear fall in fluorescence intensity, the lifetime dropping from 627 to 137 microseconds, the separated radiative and nonradiative rates, the quantum yield - is measured. The multiconfigurational calculation contributes exactly one negative claim: that the earlier published density functional work overestimated the influence of the U-Cl bond on the U-O bond. Nothing about the pressure behaviour itself is computed. The active-space issue is that the selection criterion is tied to one of the two bonds being compared. The space is specified by a procedure rather than a count: 'the active spaces selected included the f and d orbitals of the U atom that had significant bonding with the O atoms.' The orbitals were therefore chosen for their U-O bonding significance, and the conclusion drawn is about U-Cl covalency. A space assembled from uranium f and d orbitals selected by their overlap with the oxo oxygens is not one in which U-Cl bonding is guaranteed to be representable, so the observation that CASSCF orbitals show less chloride involvement than density functional orbitals partly reflects what the space was allowed to contain rather than an independent verdict on covalency. What may legitimately be inferred is that the two methods place different amounts of chloride character in the frontier orbitals; what may not be inferred without the missing details is that the CASSCF value is the converged one. And the missing details are extensive. The body text gives no electron count, no orbital count, no list of which f and d orbitals met the criterion, no root count, no multiplicities, no state-averaging scheme, and no perturbative correction of any kind - the wave functions are bare CASSCF, so dynamic correlation is absent from the densities the topological analysis reads. Nor is it stated whether the basis used for the correlated step is the one quoted for the preceding hybrid-functional calculation that supplied the starting orbitals. There is, however, a real external validation: the covalency degree computed for the U-O bond at the experimental geometry is compared against the experimentally determined charge density, giving -0.92 against -0.93, about one percent error. That anchors the derived quantity to a measurement rather than to another calculation - though it validates a single point, not the trend across the scan, which is what the paper's argument rests on. Geometries are imposed by hand: the U-O distance is stepped through 1.75-1.80 angstrom and the U-Cl distance through 2.40-2.68 angstrom in sequential scans, nothing is optimized, and the authors explicitly disclaim predictive force - 'this does not predict what will occur under pressure'. A model-boundary point beyond the space: the experiment is on a crystalline solid under gigapascal pressure, while the calculation is on an isolated dianionic complex ion in vacuum, with no lattice, no cesium counterions and no embedding field. Pressure cannot enter such a model at all; it enters only as the hand-chosen bond lengths. The proposed physical explanation for the quenching - increased nonradiative relaxation through phonon modes - is by construction outside anything the molecular calculation can address, and is offered as inference from the measured rates. The paper also disagrees with earlier published work on the same system computed at a different level.

The multiconfigurational calculations enter only through the topological bonding analysis of the isolated complex anion at hand-set bond lengths; all pressure-dependent observables are experimental. No point group is stated; the isolated complex anion is taken from the monoclinic C2/m structure of Cs2UO2Cl4 but is treated without lattice, counterions or embedding field. Two ten-electron twelve-orbital variants add either four acetate pi orbitals or four orbitals carrying acetate sigma contributions.
active_space_protocol: The paper is a systematic study of how the active space and the orbitals chosen for it control a computed exchange coupling, and it is worth recording in detail. The minimal space is two electrons in the two singly occupied metal-d-based magnetic orbitals. Three enlargements were tested on the first complex: adding the two doubly occupied and four virtual d-z-squared- and d-based orbitals gives six electrons in eight orbitals - and the paper notes the d-z-squared orbitals must be included or the calculation will not converge to the intended solution; adding four acetate pi orbitals gives ten in twelve; adding four acetate sigma orbitals instead gives a different ten in twelve. The results order the enlargements clearly: the eight-orbital space barely changes the coupling, the pi extension changes it little, and only the sigma extension improves matters materially - the bridging sigma pathway is what carries the coupling. Equally important is the choice of orbitals within the minimal space: state-specific and 50/50-averaged orbitals give couplings far too small, while orbitals from a 70/30 average of the two lowest singlets, which have substantially larger delocalization tails onto the bridging ligands, do much better and are cheaper than any enlargement. The sigma-extended solution proved fragile - only one of the two possible solutions could be converged for three of the complexes and none at all for two others - and further enlargement was prohibitively costly. This complex is the one on which the full series of active-space tests was run.
nroots_per_mult: the lowest singlet and triplet; the orbitals were obtained state-specifically and from state averages weighted 50/50 and 70/30
electronic_structure_description: The ground state is the singlet of an antiferromagnetically coupled copper pair. Computed couplings from the minimal space are -19 cm-1 at the reference level and -69, -41 or -124 cm-1 after the perturbative correction depending on whether state-specific, 50/50-averaged or 70/30-averaged orbitals are used. Enlarging the space gives -89 cm-1 for the eight-orbital case, -93 for the pi extension and -140 for the sigma extension. The configuration-interaction treatment gives -142 cm-1 from the averaged orbitals and -167 from natural orbitals, rising to -265 and -243 once the full-configuration-interaction correction is applied. Broken-symmetry density functional theory gives -229 or -450 cm-1 depending on the mapping formula used.
Other: The corrected configuration-interaction value of -265 cm-1 matches a published result of -271 cm-1 from the same procedure. Earlier configuration-interaction studies of this same complex gave -195 to -239 cm-1 with different basis sets and a different code, from which the authors conclude that both basis set and the details of how the method is implemented can shift the computed coupling substantially - a caution about comparing such numbers across papers.

geometry_source: minimum-energy crossing point (MECP) geometries optimized in this work. XMS-CASPT2 and CASSCF intersections were located with analytical nonadiabatic coupling matrix elements and the Bearpark gradient-projection algorithm; the SF-TDDFT comparisons additionally used penalty-constrained and branching-plane algorithms that avoid explicit nonadiabatic couplings, all within the Tamm-Dancoff approximation
method: XMS-CASPT2 and CASSCF as the multireference references for S1/S0 minimum-energy conical intersection geometries, compared against spin-flip TDDFT with the BHHLYP (50 percent Hartree-Fock exchange) and wB97X functionals
software: BAGEL for the XMS-CASPT2 conical-intersection optimizations; Molpro 2015.1 for the CASSCF ones; Q-Chem for the DFT and SF-TDDFT calculations
basis_set: cc-pVDZ
active_space_protocol: (6,6) with the cc-pVDZ basis, taken from the published studies of each molecule's conical intersection rather than re-derived - the aim was to reproduce well-known MECPs, not to find new ones. Note that the paper flags some of these as reduced spaces forced by technical limitations. The paper's own warning about active spaces, worth carrying: the success of CASSCF and by extension XMS-CASPT2 for conical-intersection geometries is limited by the active space, which in turn is limited either by an inexperienced user or by software constraints. Their concrete example is 9H-adenine, where the original authors were forced down to (6,6) for the intersection search even though they had identified (12,10) as the correct space. Geometrical parameters lying along the g and h branching vectors are expected to be well described by CASSCF, but other bond lengths can come out too long - differences between CASSCF and XMS-CASPT2 geometries were found in several cases, 9H-adenine among them.
Other: One of nine molecules in the paper's Table 1 benchmark of conical-intersection geometry methods.

compound_name: Complex 3a, cerium-rhodium heterometallic cluster with multiple Ce-Rh bonds
metal_center: Ce, together with three Rh centres
metal_ox_state: Not a single number: CASSCF gives a multiconfigurational ground state that is 68 percent Ce(III) and 32 percent Ce(IV), so the cerium is intermediate-valent rather than one or the other. The rhodium centres are assigned as Rh(I) with one Rh(0).
d_electron_count: For cerium the relevant count is the 4f occupancy, which is fractional here - between the 4f1 of Ce(III) and the 4f0 of Ce(IV)
ligand_set: A tripodal triamido-phosphine framework, N[(CH2CH2NPiPr2)]3, bridging the cerium to three rhodium centres, with cyclooctadiene on the rhodium in the precursor. The reduction removes the chlorides and forms direct Ce-Rh and Rh-Rh bonds.
geometry_source: Optimized in this work with the B3PW91 density functional, and validated against the single-crystal structure: computed against experimental metal-metal distances are 2.85 against 2.8360(4), 3.14 against 3.1553(4), 2.85 against 2.8068(4), 2.67 against 2.6871(4) and 2.96 against 2.9345(4) Angstrom for the five Ce-Rh and Rh-Rh contacts. No geometry is optimized at the multiconfigurational level.
method: B3PW91 density functional theory for geometries, spin densities and natural bond orbital analysis, with CASSCF called in specifically to settle the cerium oxidation state. The effective-core-potential strategy runs two ways: small-core relativistic effective core potentials keep the 4f shell in the valence and let the calculation decide the occupancy, while large-core potentials are, in the authors' words, 'dedicated to a given oxidation state' and so must be run twice, once assuming Ce(III) and once Ce(IV). The two treatments were first benchmarked against the precursor complexes where the oxidation states are unambiguous. Experimental support comes from X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, XANES, single-crystal diffraction and SQUID magnetometry.
relativistic_treatment: Relativistic effective core potentials on the rare earth centres, used in both small-core and large-core forms as a deliberate probe of the oxidation state. No treatment is described for the CASSCF step specifically.
active_space_orbital_description: Only counts are given, never compositions. Three spaces were tried - CAS(3,3), CAS(3,7) and CAS(7,7) - and no orbital is named or depicted for any of them in the article. The adopted minimal space is recorded here as (3,3).
active_space_protocol: An enlargement test was run, varying both axes, though reported in a single sentence: 'Several active spaces were considered to compute the ground state in order to define the most appropriate one. The small CAS(3,3) was found to be leading to similar results than larger CAS(3,7) or even CAS(7,7), and all are giving a doublet ground state for complex 3a with a multiconfigurational ground state formed by 68% Ce(III) and 32% Ce(IV).' Going from (3,3) to (3,7) adds orbitals at fixed electron count, and from (3,7) to (7,7) adds electrons at fixed orbital count, so the two directions of enlargement are probed separately. All three agree. Not given: any composition for any space, a root count, a basis set, software, a perturbative correction, or a statement of how the 68/32 weights were extracted from the wave function.
multiplicities_studied: Doublet ground state, obtained consistently from all three active spaces
electronic_structure_description: An intermediate-valence cerium problem in which two independent structural readings contradict each other. On one side, the unpaired spin density shows depletion at cerium and accumulation at rhodium, and large-core calculations assuming Ce(IV) give a doublet with 0.84 unpaired electrons on one rhodium and reproduce the metal-metal distances better than the Ce(III) assumption does, so 'one can therefore conclude that there is a Ce(IV) center present with one Rh(0)'. On the other, 'the RE-N bond distances in complex 3a are found to lie in between the bond distances found for the La(III) and Nd(III) complexes, so that one may conclude that this is compatible with a Ce(III) center'. The CASSCF ground state is a doublet whose wave function is 68 percent Ce(III) and 32 percent Ce(IV), so both structural signatures are partly right. The calculation was triggered by an experimental anomaly: among all the complexes measured, the cerium one alone has a chi-T versus temperature curve that 'is not smooth and is the only one to exhibit a change in slope, indicative to some extent of temperature independent paramagnetism and of a multiconfigurational ground state'. The multireference result accounts for that slope change and matches the Ce(IV) fingerprints seen in XANES. The effect is specific to cerium: the singly occupied orbital of the neodymium analogue and the highest occupied orbital of the lanthanum one show no such delocalization toward rhodium. Bonding indices give a strongly polarized Ce-Rh bond at 0.51 with Rh-Rh values of 0.40, 0.37 and 0.18.
Other: A null result from a test that varies both axes separately, licensing a minimal space for this property. CAS(3,3), CAS(3,7) and CAS(7,7) all return the same doublet ground state and the same 68 to 32 mixture of Ce(III) and Ce(IV). The progression is well chosen: (3,3) to (3,7) adds four orbitals while holding the electron count, and (3,7) to (7,7) adds four electrons while holding the orbital count, so orbital-space and electron-count enlargement are probed independently and neither moves the answer. The qualification is how little else is disclosed. No orbital is named for any of the three spaces, so a reader cannot tell what the (3,3) contains, nor what the four added orbitals in (3,7) were. No basis set, no software, no root count and no perturbative correction are given, and the article does not say how the 68 to 32 weights were extracted. The agreement across three spaces is an internal consistency check on a calculation whose setup is not documented.
reference_short: Shi, Douair, Feng, Wang, Zhao, Maron & Zhu, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2021, 143, 5998
notes: A synthesis and characterization Article reporting the first molecule with multiple rare-earth to rhodium bonds, seven authors across two groups with two corresponding. The multireference supplies the 68 to 32 mixture that reconciles two structural observables pointing to different cerium oxidation states, which a single-determinant calculation cannot do, since such a calculation must place the 4f electron either on cerium or not. It also accounts for an experimental magnetic anomaly, the slope change and temperature-independent paramagnetism unique to the cerium member, and agrees with the Ce(IV) fingerprints in XANES. The multireference covers only the cerium complex. The neodymium and lanthanum analogues 3b and 3c are computed by density functional theory alone, and their frontier orbitals show none of the delocalization toward rhodium that the cerium complex does; they receive no rows. The entry is marked partial on several counts. Compound 3a is identified only by its label - no molecular formula is given in the text and the authors describe its formation mechanism as 'ambiguous' - so the row is written under the paper's own label with no structure guessed. Beyond that, no basis set, no software, no root count and no active-space composition appear anywhere in the article, with computational details listed among the Supporting Information contents. On the density functional side, small-core effective core potentials keep the 4f shell in the valence so the calculation can decide its occupancy, whereas large-core potentials are 'dedicated to a given oxidation state' and must be run twice under opposite assumptions. The two were benchmarked against the precursor complexes, where the oxidation states are unambiguous and the computed spin densities of 1.02 for cerium and 3.06 for neodymium confirm the expected assignments. Complex 3a was obtained by reducing the chloride-bridged precursor 2a, Ce{N[(CH2CH2NPiPr2)RhCl(COD)]3}, with potassium graphite. The paper states that 'the detailed mechanism for the formation of complex 3a is ambiguous' but probably involves reduction of two Rh(I) to Rh(0), oxidative addition of two C-H bonds on the cyclooctadiene, and reductive elimination. The density functional side is described only in terms of its effective core potentials - small-core for cerium and neodymium, and eleven-electron large-core potentials in the comparison runs - with no orbital basis specified. No CASPT2, NEVPT2 or any other correction is applied on top of the CASSCF, so the 68 to 32 configuration weights come from a bare multiconfigurational wave function; the three-space agreement tests the reference space rather than what a correction would do to it.

compound_name: trans-nitrofurantoin, a widely used urinary-tract antibiotic and an environmental contaminant, studied for the channels open after photoabsorption
geometry_source: ground-state minimum from a hybrid functional; conical intersections optimized multiconfigurationally starting from geometries where trajectories actually hopped; reaction pathways built from the vertical region to those crossings
method: a staged protocol: state-averaged complete active space self-consistent field with a small space and basis to drive exploratory surface-hopping dynamics, then the hopping geometries clustered by unsupervised machine learning, then conical intersections optimized and reaction paths built with a larger space, more states and a better basis at both the self-consistent-field and multistate perturbation levels
software: not named in the extracted text
basis_set: 6-31G for the exploratory dynamics; 6-31G* for the production conical-intersection optimizations and pathway calculations
relativistic_treatment: none
active_space_nel: 12 in the exploratory dynamics, 16 in the production calculations
active_space_norb: 9 in the exploratory dynamics, 11 in the production calculations
active_space_orbital_description: the production space comprises six pi orbitals, three pi-star orbitals and two n orbitals; the smaller exploratory space is not broken down by type
active_space_protocol: Two spaces used in sequence, and the paper is unusually explicit about why a single space would not do. The difficulty it states is real: the bright state is neither the first nor the second excited state, so many states must be carried, and convergence of smooth surfaces demands averaging over still more states than the mechanism itself needs - all of which is unaffordable at the production level across thousands of trajectory steps. The resolution is to use a twelve-electron nine-orbital space with a minimal basis and only two or three averaged states to find where the molecule actually goes, then rebuild the important geometries and paths in a sixteen-electron eleven-orbital space with six averaged states and a polarized basis. The number of averaged states is varied deliberately within the production space too - three for the ground-to-first-excited crossings, four for the first-to-second, six for the higher ones - matched to which states are degenerate at each crossing. The authors also concede the compromise in the dynamics: trajectories were launched only from low-lying states and higher-energy channels reached by scaling the initial velocities, because starting from the genuinely relevant high states was not affordable.
nroots_per_mult: two or three states averaged in the exploratory dynamics; three to six in the production calculations depending on which crossing is being optimized
electronic_structure_description: Four reaction channels emerge. The first is photolytic: one N-O bond of the nitro group breaks, and the dissociation limit is strongly multireference because of near-degenerate states there. The second is a large-amplitude isomerization about the central C-N bond. The third combines pyramidalization at the nitro nitrogen with internal rotation of the nitro group about the C-N bond. The fourth is governed by bending of the O-N-O angle. Crossings were located between the ground and first excited state, between the first and second, between the second and third, and between the third and fourth.
Other: The machine-learning step is what makes the protocol work rather than an ornament: every geometry at which a trajectory hopped from the first excited state to the ground state was collected, then reduced in dimension and clustered, and the distinct clusters identified which conical intersections were worth optimizing. That replaces guessing the reactive coordinates in advance, which the authors note they had no basis for - the system is too large and its transitions too tangled for chemical intuition to supply the relevant coordinates.
reference_short: Lin, Hu, Peng, Xu, Gu and Lan, Chemosphere 281, 130831 (2021)
notes: The compound is studied as an environmental pollutant rather than as a drug - the question is what it does when sunlight reaches it in water. A flow chart of the staged protocol is given in the paper, and the active-space orbitals in the supporting information. One test finding worth noting: when the initial velocities were scaled by a factor of three, every trajectory gave oxygen-atom detachment, so the higher-energy channels are reachable but only by supplying energy the thermal sampling does not provide.
correlation_correction: multistate second-order perturbation theory on the production reference, used for the vertical excitation energies and for the reaction pathways

Where CASPT2-SO nevertheless agrees well, the paper credits the active space rather than the correction, attributing its good group-13 numbers to a much larger active space than the valence s and p set used here. And the value of the correction reverses by group for a stated reason: in groups 13 and 14 the lower-angular-momentum states lie lower, external correlation matters, and the on-top functional cuts the error from about 18-22 percent to about 4-9 percent; in groups 16 and 17 the higher-angular-momentum states lie lower so the ground state is more degenerate, static correlation dominates, bare X2C-CASSCF is already accurate to about 5-11 percent, and the correction then leaves the answer essentially unchanged. A pathology is reported openly: for gold the on-top step breaks the J symmetry the variational reference had right, splitting the 2D(5/2) level so that MJ = +/-5/2 falls about 207 meV below MJ = +/-1/2, so a range rather than a single number has to be quoted.

metal_ox_state: +1 in the entrance/product catalyst and +3 in the oxidative-addition intermediate
ligand_set: two beta-diketonate-derived O,O/C-bound ligands around Cu, plus iodobenzene in the entrance complex; oxidative addition gives Cu(III)-phenyl/iodide coordination and reductive elimination forms the arylated beta-diketone product
point_group: No symmetry constraint is stated; all molecular geometries and reaction paths were treated without imposed point-group symmetry.
geometry_source: Stationary points were optimized with omega-B97XD/SDD(Cu,I)/6-31G(d)(C,H,O), PCM(DMSO), and verified by frequencies/IRCs. CASSCF/CASPT2 energies were evaluated on these DFT geometries and along the DFT IRCs. The attached 41-atom XYZ is the ESI's exact omega-B97XD singlet PhI...b entrance-complex geometry used as the CASSCF/CASPT2(12,12) reactant structure; it is not represented as a CASSCF-optimized geometry.
method: Ground-state CASSCF(12e,12o)/CASPT2 single-point energy profiles on DFT-optimized geometries and DFT IRC points for Cu-catalysed oxidative addition and reductive elimination in PCM DMSO; separate singlet and triplet CASPT2 profiles; CASPT2 comparison of oxidative-addition/reductive-elimination, iodine-atom-transfer, and single-electron-transfer precursors. B3LYP-D3, omega-B97XD, PBE0, TPSS, and MN15 geometries were benchmarked, with omega-B97XD selected for the detailed CASSCF/CASPT2, MP2, and CCSD comparisons.
software: Molcas 8.4 for CASSCF/CASPT2; Gaussian 16 Revision B.01 for DFT optimizations, frequencies, IRCs, PCM, MP2, and CCSD
basis_set: CASSCF/CASPT2 stationary-point energies: Stuttgart/Dresden valence bases with ECP10MDF on Cu and ECP46MWB on I, and cc-pVTZ on C, H, and O. CASPT2 evaluations along the OA/RE IRCs used cc-pVDZ on non-Cu/I atoms to reduce cost after a cc-pVDZ/cc-pVTZ test showed sub-1-kcal mol-1 activation-energy differences. DFT structures used the same Cu/I ECP bases and 6-31G(d) on other atoms; DFT energy evaluations used 6-311+G(d,p).
relativistic_treatment: Stuttgart/Dresden ECP10MDF replaces 10 Cu core electrons and ECP46MWB replaces 46 I core electrons; the source gives no further decomposition of scalar-relativistic effects.
active_space_orbital_description: A Cu double-shell core of five occupied 3d orbitals plus five correlating 3d-prime/nominal 4d orbitals, augmented by one occupied and one unoccupied reaction-specific pair. In the OA sequence that pair follows the C-I/Cu-C bond-cleavage/formation channel (represented at some geometries by a Cu 3p-like orbital and partner); in the RE sequence it follows the Cu-C/C-C bond-breaking/forming sigma and sigma* channel. Orbital identity was tracked consistently from the transition-state-defined space along each IRC.
active_space_protocol: Source-explicit convergence test: CAS(10e,10o), containing only the five Cu 3d and five correlating 3d-prime orbitals, was compared directly with CAS(12e,12o), which adds the occupied/unoccupied reaction-bond pair. The two CASPT2 energy profiles were quantitatively alike, but CAS(12,12) was retained as the converged production space because it explicitly represents bond cleavage/formation. For separated mechanistic precursors, fragment spaces were chosen to total 12e,12o: b CAS(10,10)+PhI CAS(2,2), d CAS(11,11)+Ph radical CAS(1,1), and f CAS(9,9)+PhI radical CAS(3,3).
nroots_per_mult: Separate ground singlet and triplet CASSCF/CASPT2 energy profiles; no state averaging or excited-state root count is reported.
electronic_structure_description: The productive singlet cycle is oxidative addition followed by reductive elimination; the triplet surface remains well above it and no singlet-triplet crossing was found (CASPT2 singlet-triplet gap at Cu(III) intermediate c: 36.2 kcal mol-1). On omega-B97XD geometries, CASPT2 gives an 8.6 kcal mol-1 OA barrier and a 5.3 kcal mol-1 RE barrier from c, so OA is rate-determining. Cu d population falls from about 9.90 to 9.46 during OA and rises from 9.51 to 10.00 during RE. The key occupied Cu 3d-pi natural orbital drops from occupation 1.98 to 1.86 while its partner rises 0.02 to 0.14 toward Cu(III), then returns toward 1.98/0.02 during RE. This reflects 3d-pi mixing with C-I sigma* in OA and Cu-C sigma* in RE. Hartree-Fock configuration weights remain 0.914-0.954, showing mostly single-reference character despite the larger Cu(III) static-correlation signature.
Other: The CAS(10,10)->CAS(12,12) comparison is entered as an active-space protocol because the ESI explicitly describes it as a convergence test. CASPT2 reference weights are 0.454-0.466 for the 134 correlated electrons; the authors compare this with an expected 0.27-0.51 range and regard the 0.1 au imaginary shift as successfully suppressing intruders. The ESI warns that separated-fragment CASPT2 reaction energies are not quantitatively size-extensive when strong correlation appears. All precursor complexes, OA/RE intermediates and transition states, rejected IAT/SET/sigma-metathesis branches, DFT functional variants, IRC points, oxidation states, and spin surfaces belong to one atom-conserving coupling reaction and are consolidated into this single row rather than over-split.

geometry_source: initial geometries and velocities sampled from the Wigner distribution without temperature broadening using SHARC tools; 100 trajectories propagated for 150 fs with a 0.5 fs time step
method: trajectory surface hopping (fewest switches, energy-based decoherence correction with a 0.1 Hartree decay factor) with XMS-CASPT2 using analytical nonadiabatic coupling vectors as the reference, compared against XMS-CASPT2 with local diabatization, MS-CASPT2, CASSCF, CC2, ADC(2), CIS, and TD-/TDA-DFT (PBE, PBE0, CAM-B3LYP)
software: SHARC for the dynamics; BAGEL for the reference XMS-CASPT2 (NACV and local diabatization); OpenMolcas for XMS-CASPT2 (lLD), MS-CASPT2 and CASSCF with the RI approximation and analytical Cholesky decomposition; Turbomole 7.3 for CC2 and ADC(2); Gaussian 16, Turbomole and ORCA 5.0.3 for the CIS and DFT variants
basis_set: def2-SVP for every benchmarked method
active_space_orbital_description: the pi and pi* orbitals plus the two nitrogen lone pairs
active_space_protocol: (6,4): pi, pi* and the two nitrogen lone pairs, used identically for XMS-CASPT2, MS-CASPT2 and CASSCF so the methods are compared on equal footing. The reference XMS-CASPT2 used no level shift and had IPEA deactivated. Note the independent convergence on this same (6,4) space for azomethane in 10.1021/acs.jctc.9b00917 and 10.1021/acs.jctc.3c00137, though those papers do not all spell out the orbital composition
Other: Reference XMS-CASPT2 dynamics resolves four time regimes: (I) about 30 fs during which all molecules stay cis on S1; (II) crossing of a first conical intersection region up to about 60 fs, giving 20-25 percent nonadiabatic S1-to-S0 decay and complete cis-to-trans isomerization; (III) a roughly 40 fs plateau with most molecules trans; (IV) a second strong-coupling region with further decay, during which some molecules return to cis. The 90 degree conical intersection is reached after about 40 fs and the 270 degree one from about 120 fs. The end of regime II appears at about 60 fs regardless of electronic structure method. Method verdict: multireference methods are the preferred choice. CC2, TD-PBE, TDA-PBE, TD-PBE0 and TD-CAM-B3LYP are too unstable near electronic degeneracies to give trustworthy statistics. ADC(2) with local diabatization, TDA-PBE0 and TDA-CAM-B3LYP reproduce the timescale (despite up to 40 percent of trajectories crashing) but predict almost total decay through the first crossing and so badly describe the 'rotator' trajectories. CIS additionally fails to reproduce the population plateau. The authors' most transferable caution: which methods would succeed could hardly be predicted from a static analysis of the potential energy surfaces, so the usual practice of validating an electronic structure method on static energetics before running dynamics may not be sufficient.
reference_short: Which Electronic Structure Method to Choose in Trajectory Surface Hopping Dynamics Simulations? Azomethane as a Case Study, J. Phys. Chem. Lett. (2024)
notes: Metal-free organic (metal_center = none). compound_name: LiCl, gas-phase complex of a chlorine with a cluster of 1 lithium atom
geometry_source: the lithium cluster geometry optimized at Hartree-Fock in a cc-pVDZ basis starting from published structures, then a rigid scan of the distance between the chlorine and its nearest lithium atom, each point seeded from the converged result of the previous separation
method: CONSTRAINED CASSCF with two electrons in two orbitals, in which the total population of the active space on the molecular fragment is held to a chosen value so that the space is forced to span both the chlorine and the metal cluster; a dynamic weighting parameter is used to keep the surfaces smooth and the optimization convergent
basis_set: cc-pVDZ, used both for the Hartree-Fock cluster geometry optimizations and for the constrained CASSCF surfaces
relativistic_treatment: none; light main-group atoms
active_space_orbital_description: two electrons in two orbitals, defined NOT by naming orbitals but by a population constraint - the active space must carry a specified total projected weight on the molecular fragment, implemented through a projector after symmetric orthogonalization of the atomic basis. Without that constraint 'both active orbitals would be located on the lithium cluster'. With it, and although the constraint fixes only the SUM, one active orbital comes out on the lithium cluster and the other on the chlorine. For display the orbitals were localized by diagonalizing the projector onto the molecule, an analysis step that changes no energy since the results 'depend only on the active space and are invariant to the choice of individual orbitals'
active_space_protocol: a CONSTRAINED rule rather than a selection rule: rather than choosing which orbitals enter, the calculation fixes a physical property of the space - its population on one fragment - and lets the orbital optimization proceed subject to that. The single empirical parameter is the dynamic weighting factor, set to 0.37 'to match the energy gap of the crossing as well as provide appropriate weights to ensure convergence' and then varied from 0.037 to 1.47 as a sensitivity check
multiplicities_studied: the two lowest states of the combined system, treated together
nroots_per_mult: two states are optimized under dynamic weighting - the ground state and the charge-transfer state; a larger manifold of bath states arising from single excitations is examined separately
electronic_structure_description: A donor-acceptor pair whose two lowest states cross as the chlorine is pulled away from the metal cluster - one state with the transferring electron on the cluster and one with it on the chlorine, the crossing between them being the electron-transfer event. The crossing moves outward as the cluster grows, which the paper traces to the falling ionization potential of larger clusters through a near-linear relationship between the two, while the bond energy stays essentially constant across the whole series so that 'the energy of the bond is quite local'. The diabatic coupling behaves in two opposite ways depending on where it is evaluated: measured AT the crossing it falls exponentially with cluster size, because the crossing itself recedes; measured at its maximum along the coordinate it 'does not change dramatically'. Beyond these two states lies a manifold of bath states from single excitations, whose coupling to the charge-transfer state sets a resonance width and hence a lifetime

An unconstrained two-electron, two-orbital space on a chlorine-plus-lithium-cluster system puts everything on the metal, so it cannot describe the transfer of an electron between the two fragments at all - the quantity the whole study is about would be identically absent. The variational principle actively drives the space onto one site, and the paper's entire methodological contribution exists to prevent that. THE REMEDY is A new kind of selection rule: A constraint on the active space's population rather than on the identity or count of its orbitals. Since the calculation 'must be sure that the active space spans both the molecule and the metal', the authors 'enforce the constraint that the total population on the molecule for the active space' takes a chosen value, implemented after symmetric orthogonalization of the atomic basis and expressed through a projector. The constraint is weaker than the outcome it produces: 'the space of active orbitals must contain the same total projected magnitude onto the lithium orbitals and chlorine orbitals, but there is no reason to assume that one active orbital must be localized on the chlorine and the other on the lithium cluster. Nevertheless, for the most part... we do find that one active orbital is located on the lithium cluster and the other is localized on the chlorine.' A condition on the SUM delivers a one-orbital-per-fragment arrangement without demanding it, so the donor-acceptor picture emerges from the calculation rather than being imposed on it. The paper also states plainly the principle this whole collection depends on: 'within a CASSCF calculation, the results depend only on the active space and are invariant to the choice of individual orbitals'. The active orbitals are then localized by diagonalizing the projector onto the molecule purely so that they can be looked at - an analysis step with no effect on any energy. The one empirical parameter is sensitivity-tested over A fortyfold range and the two observables respond differently. The dynamic-weighting parameter was 'chosen empirically to match the energy gap of the crossing as well as provide appropriate weights to ensure convergence', which is frank about its arbitrariness. Varying it from 0.037 to 1.47 leaves the crossing position essentially fixed - 'for all values, the crossing sits around 7.7 angstrom' in the three-lithium case - while 'the diabatic coupling strength does depend on the weighting parameter, but the change is no more than 50 percent'. The geometric conclusion is therefore independent of the fitted parameter while the magnitude of the coupling is not. The size dependence differs with where the coupling is measured: 'the strength at the crossing decreases exponentially with the increase of the lithium atom number while the maximum coupling does not change dramatically'. The two are not in conflict - the crossing point itself moves to larger separations as the cluster grows, so an exponentially decaying coupling evaluated at a receding point falls exponentially while its peak value barely moves. Anyone quoting 'the diabatic coupling versus cluster size' from this system must say which of the two they mean. The physical effect usually invoked turns out to be the weak one: delocalization of the metal orbital over a larger cluster does reduce the overlap and hence the coupling, 'but this effect is weak (scaling as the square root of the cluster volume) and can easily be overshadowed by other geometric features that are accentuated in a cluster of a finite number of atoms'. The same conclusion returns for the state lifetime: it 'fluctuates for different clusters, indicating that the geometry of the cluster (and the position of Cl relative to the cluster) is just as important (if not more so) as the total number of atoms'. Geometry beats size, twice over. The rate-like quantity is A composite and the approximations are named. The resonance width is obtained from a golden-rule expression fed by constrained-CASSCF couplings and state densities, with the delta function replaced by a Gaussian of 0.14 electronvolts, and the authors immediately caution that 'approximating a delta function cannot be terribly reliable until the cluster size is quite large'. Cluster geometries and all ionization potentials come from Hartree-Fock, and a local density of states is separately built from Hartree-Fock orbital energies specifically to connect with solid-state practice, where 'multireference calculations are rare and lifetimes are calculated (almost by default) using local densities of states'. The paper limits itself explicitly: 'in principle, Gamma must converge to a fixed value as we increase the cluster size, but clearly we have not yet reached the bulk limit (and reaching such a limit will require a more optimized code implementation on our end)'. A study whose stated purpose is the transition from homogeneous to heterogeneous electron transfer, saying openly that it has not reached the heterogeneous end, is reporting its own incompleteness rather than extrapolating past it

Varying it from 0.037 to 1.47 leaves the crossing position essentially fixed - 'for all values, the crossing sits around 7.7 angstrom' in the three-lithium case - while 'the diabatic coupling strength does depend on the weighting parameter, but the change is no more than 50 percent'. The geometric conclusion is therefore independent of the fitted parameter while the magnitude of the coupling is not. The size dependence differs with where the coupling is measured: 'the strength at the crossing decreases exponentially with the increase of the lithium atom number while the maximum coupling does not change dramatically'. The two are not in conflict - the crossing point itself moves to larger separations as the cluster grows, so an exponentially decaying coupling evaluated at a receding point falls exponentially while its peak value barely moves. Anyone quoting 'the diabatic coupling versus cluster size' from this system must say which of the two they mean. The physical effect usually invoked turns out to be the weak one: delocalization of the metal orbital over a larger cluster does reduce the overlap and hence the coupling, 'but this effect is weak (scaling as the square root of the cluster volume) and can easily be overshadowed by other geometric features that are accentuated in a cluster of a finite number of atoms'. The same conclusion returns for the state lifetime: it 'fluctuates for different clusters, indicating that the geometry of the cluster (and the position of Cl relative to the cluster) is just as important (if not more so) as the total number of atoms'. Geometry beats size, twice over. The rate-like quantity is A composite and the approximations are named. The resonance width is obtained from a golden-rule expression fed by constrained-CASSCF couplings and state densities, with the delta function replaced by a Gaussian of 0.14 electronvolts, and the authors immediately caution that 'approximating a delta function cannot be terribly reliable until the cluster size is quite large'. Cluster geometries and all ionization potentials come from Hartree-Fock, and a local density of states is separately built from Hartree-Fock orbital energies specifically to connect with solid-state practice, where 'multireference calculations are rare and lifetimes are calculated (almost by default) using local densities of states'. The paper limits itself explicitly: 'in principle, Gamma must converge to a fixed value as we increase the cluster size, but clearly we have not yet reached the bulk limit (and reaching such a limit will require a more optimized code implementation on our end)'. A study whose stated purpose is the transition from homogeneous to heterogeneous electron transfer, saying openly that it has not reached the heterogeneous end, is reporting its own incompleteness rather than extrapolating past it

Its full manifold of excited states, the density of states near the first excited state at the equilibrium geometry, and the coupling between that state and the bath as a function of separation are all worked through on this system. The conclusion drawn from it is mechanistic: the resonance width is largest, and the excited-state lifetime therefore shortest, when the chlorine sits close to the cluster at around two to three angstrom, not in the crossing region where the diabatic coupling is small - so electron transfer is expected to occur at short separation rather than at the curve crossing. Six systems carry constrained-CASSCF potential energy surfaces and each gets a row: the odd-numbered lithium clusters from one to eleven atoms, each paired with a chlorine, scanned along the distance between chlorine and its nearest lithium. Odd cluster sizes are used throughout so that the combined system can pair its electrons. The abstract advertises clusters 'from 1 to 17' while the reported constrained-CASSCF surfaces, crossing positions and diabatic couplings all cover one to eleven; the larger sizes appear in the Hartree-Fock ionization-potential survey and the resonance-width plot. electronic_structure_description: A closed-shell hydrogen-bonded dimer whose structural hallmark the valence CASSCF gets BACKWARDS. Experiment and CCSD(T) agree that hydrogen bonding lengthens the donor O-H bond by about 0.01 angstrom and redshifts its stretch by about 100 wavenumbers - CCSD(T) placing the donor stretch at 3756 per centimetre against a monomer average of 3866, a shift of -110. Restricted Hartree-Fock, with no correlation at all, gets the sign right, lengthening the donor bond from 0.9410 to 0.9450 angstrom. The valence CASSCF shortens it, from a monomer 0.9641 to a dimer 0.9448 angstrom, a change of -0.0193. Its dimer donor bond length of 0.9448 is within 0.0002 angstrom of the Hartree-Fock value, showing the bond receives no left-right correlation at all. The acceptor bond also shortens, by -0.0011 angstrom, where RHF and CCSD(T) lengthen it by +0.0006 and +0.0008. The oxygen-oxygen separation comes out at 3.0848 angstrom against 2.9133 at CCSD(T), yet the interaction energy of -19.16 kcal/mol OVERBINDS the CCSD(T) value of -5.22 by a factor of 3.7

The valence CASSCF space here is not a truncation anyone selected - it is every valence orbital of every atom, the largest space the concept admits short of full configuration interaction. And yet 'one of the active weakly occupied dimer orbitals correlates electrons in the acceptor lone pairs, not the donor bond, which is left without left-right correlation'. The orbitals are all present and the optimizer sends the correlating power to the wrong place. Size cannot fix this, because the space is already maximal by construction; only the orbital optimization decides where within it the correlation goes, and here it decides wrongly. The failure is diagnosed by a numerical coincidence: 'the RHF and vCAS bond lengths of the donor OH bond in (H2O)2 are nearly identical, 0.9450 angstrom and 0.9448 angstrom, respectively. Together, these two results strongly suggest that the OH donor bond in the vCAS calculations is described without any left-right correlation.' A multiconfigurational calculation reproducing a Hartree-Fock bond length to two ten-thousandths of an angstrom shows the correlated method has added nothing where it was needed. The sign of the structural effect is wrong, and Hartree-Fock gets it right. Hydrogen bonding lengthens the donor bond by about 0.01 angstrom and redshifts its stretch by about 100 wavenumbers. Restricted Hartree-Fock, with no correlation whatever, reproduces the lengthening at +0.0040 angstrom; coupled cluster with singles, doubles and perturbative triples gets it right; and the valence CASSCF shortens the donor bond by 0.0193 angstrom. A method built to add correlation to Hartree-Fock here produces a worse answer than Hartree-Fock, with the opposite sign on the structural hallmark the whole field uses to identify hydrogen bonding. The acceptor bond behaves the same way, shortening by 0.0011 angstrom where RHF and CCSD(T) both lengthen it by about 0.0007. And the energetic error runs the opposite way from the structural one. The valence CASSCF oxygen-oxygen separation is 3.0848 angstrom against 2.9133 at CCSD(T), 0.17 angstrom too long, 'suggesting an underestimation of the attractive interaction'. Yet 'paradoxically, despite the overly long O-O distance, the vCAS/aVTZ interaction energy of -19.16 kcal/mol considerably overestimates the CCSD(T)/aVTZ value (-5.22 kcal/mol)' - overbinding by a factor of 3.7 while simultaneously placing the monomers too far apart. The authors name the cause: 'this overbinding is a result of the inconsistent treatment of the electronic structure of the dimer relative to the two monomers'. A space that correlates different things in the complex than in its fragments does not cancel errors on subtraction, and an interaction energy is a subtraction. The monomers are fine, which localizes the failure precisely. For isolated hydrogen fluoride the valence CASSCF lengthens the bond from the Hartree-Fock 0.8991 angstrom to a value 'that deviates from the CCSD(T) result by only 0.0034 angstrom'. The method works on the fragments and breaks on the complex, so the defect is not in the valence-space concept but in what the optimizer does with it once a second molecule is present to offer competing orbitals. The consequence for everything built on such a reference is stated in the abstract: 'this has significant implications for subsequent treatments of dynamical correlation that are based on a vCAS reference wave function'. Perturbation theory repairs a reference; it does not repair a reference that has correlated the wrong electrons. The paper is titled a cautionary tale and is entirely a negative result. Valence CASSCF is described as having 'been applied successfully to countless' systems; the contribution here is to bound that success by exhibiting a common, chemically central class of system where it fails qualitatively and to explain why

This worked because the bond orbitals could be cleanly distinguished from those involved in the C-H or N-H bonds. There is in fact more variation among full-valence MRCI results with the reference-selection threshold than between the two choices of active space. The small space carries a second practical advantage: full-valence MRCI and ACPF expansions were prohibitively long and required reference selection (keeping occupations whose spin-coupling coefficients exceeded about 0.05), whereas with the smaller spaces the entire CASSCF could be used as the reference with no selection at all. compound_name: He...He van der Waals dimer ground state (with He...H2 excited-state and hydrogen-bonded dimers as further tests)
geometry_source: interaction energy curves versus interatomic distance; van der Waals minimum near 5.6 bohr
method: supermolecular CASSCF interaction energies analyzed for their dispersion content, with a derived closed-form CAS dispersion energy (Edisp_CAS) from CAS transition density matrices; benchmarked against SAPT dispersion at the FCI level and an exact reference potential
software: Molpro (integrals, CASSCF 1- and 2-RDMs and the supermolecular CASSCF calculations); in-house code for the CAS dispersion energy
basis_set: aug-cc-pV5Z for the interaction curves; aug-cc-pVTZ for the long-range C6 analysis
active_space_orbital_description: CAS(4,4) for the dimer, dissociating to a product of CAS(2,2) monomers; larger dimer spaces up to CAS(4,28) also tested
active_space_protocol: A quantitative warning about active-space size and intermolecular dispersion. CASSCF itself recovers a PORTION of the dispersion energy, and that portion GROWS with active-space size, so naively adding a dispersion correction to a supermolecular CASSCF interaction energy double-counts intermonomer correlation by an amount that increases with the space. For He...He: CAS(4,4)+dispersion deviates from the benchmark by only 6.6% at the vdW minimum, but CAS(4,28)+dispersion OVERestimates by 72% and shifts the minimum from 5.6 to 5.3 bohr. The paper's fix (CAS+DispCAS, subtracting the dispersion already in the CASSCF energy) keeps errors under 2% at any active-space size. The complementary limitation: even CAS(4,18) recovers only about 50% of the He...He C6 coefficient (0.735 vs the reference 1.461 a.u.) and no higher Cn, because only p orbitals are in the active space. He...H2 excited-state dimers used CAS(2,5)/CAS(2,4) for the 1Sigma_u+ state and CAS(2,2) on He with CAS(2,10) on H2 for the 1Pi_u state.
Other: The study also decomposes interaction energies of hydrogen-bonded dimers (H2O...H2O, HCN...HCN and others). The overarching message for anyone choosing a CASSCF active space for intermolecular interactions: enlarging the active space captures more dispersion inside the CASSCF energy, so dispersion corrections must be made active-space-consistent or they will double-count - a counterintuitive direction, since bigger is not automatically safer here.
reference_short: How Much Dispersion Energy Is Included in the Multiconfigurational Interaction Energy? J. Chem. Theory Comput. (2020)
notes: Metal-free rare-gas/model dimers (metal_center = none). Recorded for the transferable and counterintuitive active-space caution: CASSCF partially and size-dependently recovers dispersion, so a larger active space makes naive dispersion-corrected interaction energies WORSE (He...He CAS(4,4) 6.6% error -> CAS(4,28) 72% overestimate). active_space_nel/norb hold the CAS(4,4) dimer case; the larger and He-H2 spaces are in the protocol field.

geometry_source: CCSD-optimized geometries with the same electronic basis; molecule aligned on the z-axis with the classical H at the origin and a PB4-D protonic basis centered there
method: two-step multicomponent (nuclear-electronic orbital) CASSCF with a multicomponent heat-bath-CI solver; protonic densities benchmarked against the numerically exact Fourier Grid Hamiltonian (at CCSD) and against NEO-CCSD and multicomponent OOMP2
software: locally modified Arrow (multicomponent heat-bath CI) for the CI step; locally modified PySCF for the orbital update
basis_set: cc-pVDZ on non-hydrogen atoms, cc-pV5Z on hydrogen; PB4-D protonic basis for the quantum proton
active_space_orbital_description: up to 16 electrons in 48 electronic orbitals, plus a single quantum proton in up to 13 protonic orbitals
active_space_protocol: largest electronic space (16,48); the reported series is (12,11), (12,17), (12,27), (12,46) at a fixed 13-orbital protonic space, (1,13). Multicomponent (nuclear-electronic orbital) CASSCF, in which a proton is treated quantum-mechanically alongside the electrons; active spaces are written (n,m)/(k,l) for n electrons in m electronic orbitals and k protons in l protonic orbitals. A heat-bath-CI solver enables far larger spaces than the ~1e5-configuration limit of the previous GAMESS implementation. Two active-space lessons transfer even to single-component work. First, LARGE electronic active spaces are essential for a qualitatively correct protonic density: the density error decreases monotonically as the electronic space grows, and even the largest spaces here still trail NEO-CCSD. Second, and newly shown, the PROTONIC active space can be truncated substantially with negligible loss - not all protonic orbitals need be active - which contradicts prior multicomponent CASSCF practice.
Other: Protonic density RMS error (a.u.) versus electronic active space, showing the monotonic improvement: (12,11) 0.695 (E -199.6047 Ha); (12,17) 0.560 (-199.6796); (12,27) 0.328 (-199.7879); (12,46) 0.190 (-199.8095). Electronic spaces larger than (8,27) are needed to beat multicomponent OOMP2, yet even (16,48) remains less accurate than NEO-CCSD. Protonic-space truncation for the largest electronic space: density error 0.307 -> 0.265 -> 0.190 for 4, 6, 13 active protonic orbitals, then flat - so 13 protonic orbitals suffice.
reference_short: Fajen and Brorsen, Multicomponent CASSCF Revisited: Large Active Spaces Are Needed for Qualitatively Accurate Protonic Densities, J. Chem. Theory Comput. (2021)
notes: Metal-free multicomponent (metal_center = none); the quantum proton makes this a nuclear-electronic CASSCF. Recorded for the (n,m)/(k,l) multicomponent active-space notation and the two transferable findings: large electronic spaces are mandatory for protonic densities, and the protonic active space can be truncated.

For V(acac)3 all five d orbitals are retained even by state-specific CASSCF.

Zero-field splitting D (cm-1), SA-CASSCF/CASCI -13.64, SA-CASSCF/CMS-PDFT 13.85, CASSCF/CASCI 4.90, CASSCF/CMS-PDFT 4.96, WSA-CASSCF/CASCI 6.82, WSA-CASSCF/CMS-PDFT 7.75, experiment 7.47 MC-PDFT D values from the Supporting Information, completing the nine computed combinations: 14.25 (SA-CASSCF orbitals), 5.89 (CASSCF orbitals), 9.05 (WSA-CASSCF orbitals) cm-1. Rhombic parameter |E| (cm-1) and |E/D| from SI Table S11, WSA-CASSCF/CMS-PDFT against experiment: |E| 1.68 vs 1.92, |E/D| 0.22 vs 0.26.
Other: Spin-orbit lowering of the ground state: -35 cm-1 with SA-CASSCF orbitals, -15 with CASSCF, -19 with WSA-CASSCF; SA-CASSCF badly overestimates the SOC contribution here and even gets the sign of D wrong. One of the three molecules used for the ground-state-weight sensitivity scan, which shows a discontinuous jump in D near 25 percent weight. Core finding of the study, which is about how the orbitals are optimized rather than about the active space size: state-specific CASSCF orbitals beat conventional equal-weight SA-CASSCF orbitals, but state-specific optimization can rotate d orbitals that are empty in the ground state out of the active space entirely (this happens for Cr(acac)3 and Mo(acac)3, where two unoccupied d orbitals are lost even from a good initial guess, although the SCF itself converges). The proposed weighted-state-averaged CASSCF fixes this by putting 90 percent of the weight on the lowest state of each spin manifold and spreading the remaining 10 percent evenly over the others; all five d orbitals are then retained. Mean percentage absolute deviation in D across the set: SA-CASSCF/CASCI 102 percent, SA-CASSCF/CMS-PDFT 138, CASSCF/CASCI 39, CASSCF/CMS-PDFT 90, WSA-CASSCF/CASCI 27, and WSA-CASSCF/CMS-PDFT 14 percent (mean percentage deviation 3 percent), making WSA-CASSCF/CMS-PDFT the recommended combination. active_space_protocol: minimal CAS(10,10) covering all Fe(III) 3d electrons and orbitals; initial orbitals from the model one-electron Hamiltonian followed by AVAS. Active spaces for the transition-metal complexes come exclusively from the AVAS (atomic valence active space) procedure of Sayfutyarova et al., targeting the five 3d atomic orbitals on each metal centre taken from the MINAO minimal basis; double-d-shell guesses are available the same way. The practical appeal is that for a minimal or double-d-shell TMC calculation the only strictly necessary user input is the list of metal centre indices. AVAS supplies both the space definition and starting orbitals coherent with it. For aromatic pi systems the paper uses either broken-symmetry UHF natural orbitals (UNO) or PiAS, a simplified version of the pi-orbital guess of Sayfutyarova and Hammes-Schiffer that builds an inertia tensor over the pi centres and projects the 2p components along the principal axis, so it works for arbitrarily oriented molecules. electronic_structure_description: Ground term: 1Ag
Other: The clearest result in the paper about active-orbital choice: the convergence rate of the second-order TRAH algorithm depends crucially on it. Canonical and natural active orbitals converge slowly, taking nearly 90 iterations; localized active orbitals cut that dramatically. The explanation is chemical - localization disentangles the CAS-CI Hamiltonian into weakly coupled Fe(III) monomer blocks, each qualitatively a single high-spin CSF, which are then antiferromagnetically coupled. That coupled two-monomer CSF carries 98 percent of the weight in the final CI expansion. The first-order SXPT algorithm converged steadily in 19 iterations regardless, showing the AVAS starting orbitals are well matched to the chosen space.

compound_name: Contorted push-pull naphthalenediimide (NDI) dimer PPD, in a cyclophane architecture - intramolecular singlet exciton fission
geometry_source: cofacial NDI/NDI cyclophane dimer; excimer geometry from a TDDFT scan of the center-to-center distance (3.30-3.80 A, minimum at 3.50 A)
method: state-averaged SA3-CASSCF with XMCQDPT2 (and NEVPT2) dynamic correlation; TDDFT for the excimer potential energy scan
basis_set: DZV for the SA-CASSCF/XMCQDPT2; def2-SVP for the CAS(12,10)/NEVPT2
active_space_orbital_description: the CAS(12,10)/NEVPT2 space used for the best excitation energy; the SA3-CASSCF/XMCQDPT2 analysis was run at (4,4), (6,6), (8,8) and (10,10)
active_space_protocol: An explicit active-space-size study for a singlet-fission dimer. Excitation energies rise monotonically with active-space size: the bright S2a (CT+LE) state goes 2.63 (SA3-CAS(4,4)) -> 2.77 (6,6) -> 2.71 (8,8) -> 2.90 eV (10,10). The authors argue the low-lying states are well defined by HOMO->LUMO and HOMO-1->LUMO+1 transitions with lower frontier MOs treated as a rigid core, so a space beyond (4,4) is 'not effective' for the qualitative multi-exciton picture. But for quantitative agreement with experiment they use CAS(12,10)/NEVPT2/def2-SVP, giving the bright singlet at 2.13 eV, close to the experimental 1.80 eV. So (4,4) captures the state characters and ordering while a larger (12,10) space plus NEVPT2 is needed for accurate energies - a clean illustration of the size/accuracy tradeoff. Equal-weight SA over 3 states, C1 symmetry.
electronic_structure_description: SA3-CASSCF(ne,mo)/XMCQDPT2//DZV: S1a (multi-exciton T-T/ME, dark) / S2a (CT+LE, bright) / T1 in eV - (4,4): 1.97 / 2.63 / 1.84; (6,6): 2.13 / 2.77 / 2.05; (8,8): 2.09 / 2.71 / -; (10,10): 2.24 / 2.90 / -. CAS(12,10)/NEVPT2/def2-SVP gives the bright singlet at 2.13 eV (experiment 1.80 eV). The dark ME state lies ~0.6 eV below the bright S2a, making singlet fission exoergic. Excimer-like structure (d = 3.50 A) SA-CAS(4,4)/XMCQDPT2: S1a 1.98 eV (ME), S2a 2.64 eV (CT+LE).
Other: First evidence of intramolecular singlet exciton fission in the NDI scaffold. Individually the NDI monomer (PP-NDI) does not satisfy the SF energy criterion E(S1) >= 2 E(T1) - it is endoergic - but the contorted push-pull cyclophane dimer PPD, with the shortest cofacial NDI/NDI contact, does support exoergic SF. A multi-exciton (ME/T-T pair) state sits close in energy to the local-excitation state with mixed charge-transfer character. The dimer forms an excimer-like (not a true trapping excimer) intermediate at d = 3.50 A before the ME state.
reference_short: A highly contorted push-pull naphthalenediimide dimer and evidence of intramolecular singlet exciton fission, Chem. Sci. 13, 11506 (2022)
notes: Metal-free organic dimer (metal_center = none). compound_name: Coelenterazine (CTZ) dioxetanone, the reactive bioluminescent intermediate, in the NanoLuc luciferase protein (also computed in the gas phase and in PCM for comparison)
geometry_source: QM/MM optimized in this work. The protein-solvent system was equilibrated for 10 ns of classical AMOEBA MD, the CTZ+O2 coordinates were then manually replaced by the dioxetanone, and only a 932-atom relaxed region around the chromophore was optimized (rest frozen at the snapshot); QM region 177 atoms, comprising the chromophore plus hydrogen-bonding side chains. Reactant and product were also optimized separately in the gas phase and in PCM (eps = 78.4). Reaction path by interpolation between the optimized reactant and product for each environment
method: SA-CASSCF with polarizable QM/MM embedding in the AMOEBA force field (SA-CASSCF/AMOEBA), dynamically weighted with S0 as reference state and a 3 eV bandwidth in the PCM and QM/MM calculations; minimum-energy conical intersection searches on top
software: TeraChem for the QM part coupled to OpenMM for the MM part
active_space_orbital_description: chosen to contain enough active orbitals to describe the O-O bond dissociation of the dioxetanone ring; the low-lying states it produces are n->sigma* and sigma->sigma* local excitations in the O-O bond region
active_space_protocol: (8,9) sized around the breaking O-O bond; state-averaging over four singlets and two triplets, with dynamic weights referenced to S0 using a 3 eV bandwidth. A separate, much smaller SA(2)-CASSCF(4,3)/3-21G space was used only on an HBDI-valine model to parametrize the force field and to compare link-atom schemes
nroots_per_mult: 4 singlets and 2 triplets in the state-average
Other: State characters from attach-detach density analysis at image 20 of the gas-phase path: S1, S2 and S3 are all local 1(n,sigma*) excitations in the O-O region; T1 is 3(n,sigma*) and T2 is 3(sigma,sigma*). Environment changes the picture qualitatively. In the gas phase and in PCM the S1-S0 gap closes as the O-O bond dissociates and the MECI geometry closely resembles the product; in QM/MM the S1-S0 gap no longer approaches zero along the path, S2 and S3 rise well above their gas-phase positions (they acquire core-region excitation character), and reaching the MECI requires rotating the O-C-O group by almost 90 degrees out of the dioxetanone ring plane. The MECI topology also differs: peaked in PCM, sloped in QM/MM. Protonation: unconstrained QM/MM optimization always ends with HPh protonated and D139 deprotonated; forcing the deprotonated state requires O-H distance constraints and costs 15.6 kcal/mol. The proton-transfer energy computed with AMOEBA embedding is less sensitive to QM-region size than with a fixed-charge (AMBER-FB15 / SPC-Fw / GAFF) model.

compound_name: Perfectly eclipsed pi-stacked ethylene oligomers (4, 6 and 8 units), toy models for hole and exciton migration
geometry_source: constructed models: all ethylene units at their ground-state neutral geometry, perfectly eclipsed with a uniform 4 A interplanar spacing
method: real-time CASSCF Ehrenfest electron dynamics: a fully converged CASSCF calculation is transformed to localized orbitals (hole migration) or natural bond orbitals (exciton migration), and the resulting configuration state functions are propagated in time, with nuclear motion either frozen or coupled through the Ehrenfest gradient
software: development version of Gaussian (Ehrenfest real-time CASSCF implementation)
active_space_orbital_description: one localized pi orbital per ethylene unit for hole migration; pi and pi* on each unit, obtained as natural bond orbitals, for exciton migration
active_space_protocol: sizing rule scales with the number of stacked units n: hole migration uses a doublet CAS(2n-1, n) with the n active pi orbitals localized one per ethylene unit; exciton migration uses CAS(2n, 2n) with pi and pi* per unit transformed to NBOs. The tabulated (7,4) here is the n = 4 hole-migration case. The authors note that a physically correct excited state of ethylene would need diffuse Rydberg-like functions, which this toy model deliberately neglects
multiplicities_studied: 2 — doublet for the cationic hole-migration cases; for the radical stacks the highest-spin ferromagnetic coupling was used, e.g. 2S+1 = 6 for the six-unit system, with a 2S+1 = 4 case also run
Other: Hole migration was followed for 4, 6 and 8 units with frozen nuclei, and for 4 units with coupled nuclear motion; the transferring hole passes through a transition-state-like geometry at which the terminal A and D C=C bond lengths become equal. Coherence length is effectively infinite in this perfectly eclipsed geometry - the charge propagates across the whole stack. Results are time-dependent CSF populations, not stationary energies.

XS-CASSCF scales those exchange terms down with two parameters [mu, nu] to mimic sigma-correlation at NO extra cost - mu scales the diagonal exchange (controls the ionic S1), nu the off-diagonal coupling (controls multiconfigurational covalent states). Practical guidance the paper establishes: mu = 0.0 (simply dropping the exchange integral g_pq,qp) is usually optimal and makes the S1 energy independent of the exchange integral, halving the CASSCF singlet-triplet gap to one exchange integral rather than two; nu = 0.0 is best when only the HOMO-LUMO transition matters, but nu = 0.5-0.7 is safer when higher multiconfigurational covalent states are of interest. active_space_protocol: A minimal space: the four d electrons in the five metal d orbitals, state-averaged over 45 triplet and 5 quintet states so that the whole d-manifold is available for the spin-orbit treatment. The minimality is the paper's central methodological finding and it cuts both ways. Adding dynamic correlation perturbatively on this reference does fix the ground-state spin multiplicity, which the bare self-consistent-field calculation gets wrong, but it overestimates the quintet and singlet excited states in all four complexes and badly distorts the trigonal splitting of the lowest triplet - state-specific rather than state-averaged calculations did not help. Since both the singlet and quintet excited states matter for the low-lying spin levels, the paper concludes flatly that the perturbative correction is not applicable here in conjunction with a minimal active space. The self-consistent-field quintet energies, by contrast, are usable, and are the input to the ligand field analysis from which the magnetic parameters are derived. Doing better would mean correlating 33 electrons in 20 orbitals, which the authors call presently infeasible.

electronic_structure_description: Ground state of the d5 Cr(I) centre in a two-coordinate, quasi-linear N-Cr-N geometry. method: state-averaged complete active space self-consistent field (SA-CASSCF) with second-order N-electron valence perturbation theory (NEVPT2), in the Master matrix formalism: spin-orbit and spin-spin coupling are treated by diagonalising the Born-Oppenheimer SOC and SSC operators over the triplet and singlet roots, extended over all ms components; preliminary complete active space configuration interaction (CASCI) for the SSC contribution
electronic_structure_description: Ground term: 3A2 under D2d symmetry, from the b2^2 e^2 configuration, with the first excited state 3E (b2^1 e^3). First- and second-coordination-sphere effects give a 3A2 rather than a 3E ground state, and with it a large axial zfs. Easy-plane anisotropy: the magnetisation at 5 T reaches only 0.34 muB against a saturation value for S = 1 with g = 2.2, and fits with negative D were unsatisfactory.
Other: The (12,7) space is scanned rather than used at one geometry, and that is the paper's methodological point: along the C2v(I) -> D2d -> C2v(II) interconversion pathway D runs between 30 and 50 cm-1 for twisting angles 90 <= alpha2 <= 110 degrees, while E/D stays between 0.01 and 0.06, so the sign of D is well defined throughout and the magnitude is set by the twist. At the crystallographic angle of 98 degrees the computed D of 47.9 cm-1 and E/D of 0.05 land within 2.5 cm-1 of the FIRMS measurement. | Decomposing the computed D shows it is dominated by nickel spin-orbit coupling; the selenium donor contribution is an order of magnitude smaller and of OPPOSITE sign. The spin-spin term, from a preliminary CASCI, is only about 1 cm-1 of the 47.9 total, which is why a SOC-only treatment would still be close here.
